english: Respect for every virtue ought to flourish among the human race. People ought always to resist wrongdoing with a wise mind and win their Creator’s favor by good pursuits. Or at least, since this first and happier level of constant devotion seems both rare and exceedingly difficult, they ought to reject even long-cherished vices and return to the shelter of reform and repentance. Surely reverence for God ought at least to have remained untouched in this respect: we should not have to defend the divine law in so great a struggle. But the frenzy of sinners has reached the point where we must labor strenuously to teach that God is just. So, trusting in the help of the very justice whose cause we plead, let us now fulfill what we promised in the preceding book.

In the first book, clear definitions established that God is just in such a way that, if he could be proved unjust, he would be proved not to be God. Once no doubt remained about this, it also became clear that justice is simply the virtue that never judges unfairly or acts unfairly, but gives each person what belongs to that person, without deception or favoritism—that is, without showing partiality.

added_allusions.reason: The explanation without partiality may echo Paul’s formula concerning God’s impartiality.

english: The character of this virtue would be maintained only if God punished none of those subject to him except for offenses established to have been committed by free will.
He would not command people to do things he knew their nature made them unable to observe; nor would he judge anyone guilty for what belongs to their nature.

Nor would he charge some people with other people’s sins. Accordingly, he would not sentence innocent children to eternal punishment because of their parents’ wrongdoing, when those children had personally done nothing either good or evil by which they could be shown to have imitated their parents’ crimes. Taken together, these considerations establish both that God exists and that he is just. For it was clear that, if he did anything unjust, his divinity would suffer exactly as much damage as his fairness did.

added_allusions.reason: The children have done neither good nor evil.

translator_notes: The source attaches a comparison with Sirach 40:1 here, although its heavy-yoke language appears in Augustine’s reply, not in Julian’s words. Julian’s phrase ‘nothing either good or evil’ echoes Romans 9:11.

english: And yet—how wretched human error is!—when I consider the very subject of our dispute, I am shaken by overwhelming grief. Could this really have come into doubt? Could this cause have needed defending? Could churches professing belief in Christ, I ask, really have doubted whether God judges justly—that is, reasonably?

But my very reverence for these matters has made me forget too completely the dispute at hand. I marvel that God’s fairness could have been questioned, although it is well established that in the assemblies of the advocates of inherited sin there is no doubt at all about his unfairness.

This is worse by as much as the pursuit of evil is worse than neglect of good, as deliberate irreverence is more destructive than doubt about the truth, and, finally, as daring to accuse God is more wicked than refusing to worship him.

As the prophet David testifies, the fool did indeed say in his heart that there was no God (Psalm 14:1; Psalm 53:1; LXX/Vulgate Psalms 13:1; 52:1). Yet he did not say that God existed but was unjust. The voice of all nature declared in such harmony that justice belongs inseparably to God that someone denying his existence was more readily found than someone denying his fairness. Someone could arise who thought that what he could not see did not exist; no one had yet been found who called unjust what he believed to be divine.
That fool, then, seemed to have reached the furthest limit of wickedness by denying God. Yet a race of Manichaeans and advocates of inherited sin has been found whose irreverence surpasses his.

added_allusions.reason: Returns to the fool denying God, quoted in section 9; parallel Psalm 53:1.
Parallel occurrence of the fool denying God.

english: But to return to the point from which we digressed: it had become clear that the one we acknowledge as the true God can do nothing in judgment that conflicts with justice. Consequently, no one can be held guilty for another’s sins, and so the innocence of newborn children cannot possibly be condemned for their parents’ wrongdoing, since it would be unjust for guilt to pass through reproductive seed.

Although this is so obvious that nothing could be more decisive or more true, I had promised to prove this very point by the testimony of divine law: it would be utterly unjust to charge newborn children with their parents’ crimes. God is so opposed to this that he expressly forbade judges in his law to perpetrate anything so disgraceful. I had therefore promised to establish this. But since the second book was occupied with explaining statements of the apostle Paul, it is fitting to fulfill that promise in the opening part of this book.

We read in Deuteronomy, among the commands ordering that people’s life and conduct, that God also gave this entirely explicit command. To show where it stands among the preceding and following provisions, he says: ‘You shall not withhold the wages of a poor and needy worker, whether one of your own people or one of the foreigners living in your towns. You shall pay his wages daily; the sun must not set before you pay them, because he is poor and places his hope in them. Otherwise he may cry to the Lord against you, and you will be guilty of sin. Fathers shall not die for their children, and children shall not die for their fathers. Each person shall die for his own sin’ (Deuteronomy 24:14–16).

‘You shall not distort justice for the foreigner, orphan, or widow. You shall not take a widow’s garment as security, because you were a servant in the land of Egypt and the Lord your God freed you from there. That is why I command you to do this’ (Deuteronomy 24:17–18).

When God established the pattern for judging, he immediately took care to decree that neither parents should be struck down for their children’s crimes nor children for their parents’. He showed, then, that the first principle and starting point of the justice he commanded judges to maintain was this: family ties must not burden the innocent, and the hatred an individual had deserved must not spread to the family itself. In matters of conduct, justice therefore distinguishes those whom kinship joins. It certainly would not do so if will and reproductive seed operated on the same principle, or if an act of choice passed to descendants through reproduction. With this single testimony we have shown, more than sufficiently, that the ancient authority of the enacted law crushes the utterly repulsive corruption of judgment embraced by this new error. This pronouncement bears on the case in a way that leaves no room for doubt.

In establishing the pattern to be followed in trials, God commanded that innocence should not be implicated in the dangers faced by a relative. Just as he separated the father from the punishment of a sinful son, he separated the son from the father’s condemnation. By giving both persons the same outcome, he clearly showed that parents’ sins can no more pass to children than children’s sins pass to parents.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: Therefore, anyone who contradicts this pronouncement by saying that sin is transmitted should also say that sin travels back again. If sins descend from parents to children, let them also ascend from children to parents, since the authority of divine law shows that parents’ crimes do not harm their children, just as children’s crimes do not harm their parents.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: Anyone determined to oppose this pronouncement, then, should assert that both things happen, when both were equally forbidden. For it is easier to reject God’s law than to correct it. Rejection is irreverent, but correction is still more irreverent and absurd. If you honor one of its two decrees and detest the other, the part you accept will force you, against your will, to obey the part you reject. The dignity of the one you value also defends the one you opposed. It is completely absurd to imagine you honor commands when you dare attack part of them. Thus rejecting the whole law is more consistent than correcting it. Yet only an impious person will attempt to correct it; devout and sensible people accept and praise it in its entirety.

No one should be troubled here by seeing that the old sacrificial rites ceased in the age of the New Testament. Virtues and sacrificial victims are not governed by the same principle: commands are enduring; sacrifices are temporary. Yet when Christ came, whom the ancient sacrifices foreshadowed, what had been established was fulfilled, not condemned. Those observances are not denounced as having been practiced in their proper times; they came to rest when the perfection promised through their service arrived.

added_allusions.reason: Fulfillment rather than condemnation or abolition of the earlier law.
Ancient sacrifices foreshadow Christ and give way to fulfillment.

english: The commands containing devotion, faith, justice, and holiness, however, not only did not cease; they were increased. This law about maintaining justice in judgments, which we quoted from Deuteronomy, concerns the enduring character of commands, not the temporary age of ceremonies. It did not disappear with circumcision; it continues with justice.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: It is therefore settled—if Moses, through whom God speaks, is believed rather than Augustine, through whom Mani speaks—that children are not made guilty by nature for their parents’ sins.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: And so parents’ crimes do not pass to their descendants, although those descendants were born from them, just as children’s crimes do not pass to their parents, who certainly could not have been born from their own children. Birth, then, can no more damage someone’s innocence where that birth exists than it can where it does not exist.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: The case is settled. Still, I urge the reader to attend to what I now bring forward. Suppose someone openly professed what the advocate of inherited sin tries to establish by argument: suppose he declared war on God’s law, fearlessly despised the pronouncement we quoted, and asserted, by whatever means he could, that both requirements God wished observed were false. Suppose he did all he could to overthrow both sides of the pronouncement under discussion and fully believed that parents are and ought to be condemned for their children’s sins, and children for their parents’. Even a person like that could not establish the transmission of sin, even on his own assumptions. Why? Because even if the law’s pronouncement were proved false—the pronouncement testifying that relatives of this kind cannot be stained by each other’s crimes—it would remain unshaken that sin is not transmitted. The very fact that parental guilt passed to children and children’s guilt returned to parents would establish that birth was not what brought parents’ sins to children, since they also returned from children to parents, where birth could not be the cause.

Let the result of my argument be clear. Divine law has an inviolable authority, which no arguments of impiety can overthrow. Its decree prescribed with the greatest precision and completeness that declaring children guilty for their parents’ sin is a disgraceful opinion and a distortion of judgment, which it commanded us earnestly to avoid. This thunderbolt shattered the structure of inherited sin. Yet the faith we defend is protected by such strong defenses of truth that even the irreverence capable of denying God’s law cannot shake it.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: Now, then, let my words address the man with whom we are disputing. Do you submit to God’s law—at least in your profession, for we know what you do in argument—or do you resist it? If you submit, the dispute is over; if you resist, our agreement is over. If you submit, the error of the advocates of inherited sin is extinguished; if you resist, the unbelief of the Manichaeans is exposed. At all events, it stands established that your opinion and God’s law cannot agree.
Unless perhaps you say that God indeed commanded this, but does not do what he commanded—indeed, that he acts contrary to what he ordered others to do.

Although the extent of this irreverence is glaringly obvious as soon as it is mentioned, let us—with the permission of the very God whose fairness we defend—consider its character, even through a brief examination. What forces him to become a violator of his own law: the pressure of circumstances that overwhelm him, or his own weakness? Or, since it is neither, is it simply a desire to do wrong? But even Mani could not say this, and so he invented a story that your god had endured a terrible battle.

If neither calamity nor weakness nor a desire to transgress bears on him, how can he destroy in judging the pattern of justice he commended by commanding? Indeed, he would be raging not against that justice but against reverence for himself. For fairness has such power that it both condemns those who stray and loses none of its force through the authority of those who abandon it. How, finally, could he want us to do what is just and himself do what is unjust? Does he want us to seem more just than he is—or rather, not more just, but ourselves fair and himself unfair?
Or is what he does just—namely, charging some people with other people’s sins—while what he commands us to do is unjust: declaring each person guilty for the offenses of that person’s own will?

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: And where would such envy or malice come from in him? It is envy if he deceived his creature by his commands to prevent it from trying, as far as it could, to imitate his virtues. But it is malice—indeed cruelty—if he punishes mortals for unjust acts they committed by obeying his law.

Or perhaps he does not punish them—which is certainly prudent—but even rewards servants who obey his commands, although those commands teach injustice? Then what did his envy achieve, if mortals arrived by doing unjust things at the same destination they would have reached by observing justice? Those he deceived lose nothing of their happiness, while he is deprived both of the consciousness of goodness and justice and of the honor belonging to them. How much more tolerable it would have been to throw off the profession of religion than to steer a course along such steep and deadly paths!

Therefore, since God does not allow even his servants to commit the sort of act you claim he perpetrates himself, it is clear that you have fled from honoring him no less than from human reason. Consequently, we are not deceived, as you say, by Pelagian error; we are guided by God’s law when we maintain that it is unjust to charge children with their parents’ crimes.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: This, to our grief, is the monstrous offspring produced in our time by inherited sin, the daughter of the Manichaeans and your mother.

It has therefore become clear that God commanded what we maintain. Although the plain, genuine meaning of the pronouncement itself is accessible to everyone’s understanding and contains no blemish of obscurity, you might still take refuge in accusing us of slow intelligence and say we do not understand the command. So let us use another testimony, this time not a command but an action performed according to the command, to show how the law was understood.

In the fourth Book of Kingdoms, we read about Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah: ‘After the kingdom was firmly established in his hands, he killed his servants who had killed his father. But he did not kill their sons, in accordance with the covenant of the Lord’s law, which commands: Fathers shall not die for their children, nor children for their fathers’ (2 Kings 14:5–6). You see how the truthful historical account displays the justice of the king’s judgment. Although he had been devout, he is reported to have faltered in some respects. The authority of God’s law was therefore recalled to confirm his judgment. So that the deed should not carry too little weight because of the person who did it, it is commended as having been performed according to God’s law and covenant.

Two or three witnesses are ordinarily believed even in a case involving someone’s life. How much more should two sacred witnesses be believed when God’s honor is at stake: the law contained in Deuteronomy and the history recording the kings’ deeds! God himself prescribed how he wished judgment to be given; judgments delivered according to his law testify how his command should be understood. Is there still doubt that Scripture’s authority cannot establish the transmission of sin?

Surely the positions over which we fight such lengthy battles—what you defend and what we defend—are contrary. They are so opposed and incompatible that you fight by persecution and we by argument, you by fury and we by reason. Both sides therefore agree that these statements differ and conflict: children are punished for their parents’ sins; children are not punished for their parents’ sins. Guilt is natural; guilt is not natural. God’s law commands that parents’ sins be charged to children; God’s law commands that parents’ sins not be charged to children. It is obvious that these mutually hostile opinions and propositions cannot both be true.

The rules of trained argument also show that when two opinions arise about uncertain matters, both can be false, but both cannot be true. This can indeed occur in differing alternatives said to admit a middle position, but not in opposites that have no middle. These matters are familiar to dialecticians; for readers unfamiliar with this discipline, however, let us explain them with an example.

added_allusions.reason: Two or three witnesses in a capital case.
Two or three witnesses establish a matter.

english: Suppose, for example, the question concerns Goliath’s complexion, and one person insists he was black and another that he was white (compare 1 Samuel 17:4–5). These opposing opinions can both be false, but they cannot both be true. It cannot be true that he was black if he was always white, or that he was white if he remained black throughout his life. Thus these two opinions, which cannot both be true, can both be false if his complexion was neither white nor black but tawny—or a moderate blend of the opposites, with whiteness softened but no full blackness introduced. Differing and opposed descriptions can therefore be denied together more readily than affirmed together.

But opposites without a middle, such as good and evil, just and unjust, innocence and guilt, cannot coexist at one time in one and the same subject; so affirming either necessarily denies the other. For example, a command, advice, or assistance cannot be both just and unjust at the same time. Equally, a person cannot at one and the same time be both guilty and innocent, both good and evil.

Now apply these examples to the case. Charging children with their parents’ sins and not charging children with their parents’ sins cannot both be shown equally just. If justice consists in holding the offspring guilty, it must be injustice to declare them not guilty for those same sins. And just as it is good to command justly, it is evil to give an unjust order. Argument may weaken the force of something already obvious, yet it is helpful to confirm an established case by the supporting judgments of divine law. Let us stay with this point: anyone who stands here with a sound mind will not be allowed to wander among the precipices of our present disputes.

You therefore concede, preacher of natural evil, that God’s law commands that children must not be punished for their parents’ sins. You also acknowledge that this people understood the command precisely as we now maintain it should be observed. Consequently King Amaziah, obeying God’s commands, restrained with praiseworthy moderation the anger caused by his father’s murder. He killed his father’s assassins but spared their sons, out of justice, not cowardice. Amaziah is praised; he is said to have done this according to God’s law, and commended for obeying the Lord’s will. Yet the account does not conceal that remnants of false worship stained him, and it shows that he did not imitate the devotion of his ancestor David (2 Kings 14:3–6). Even this man, who fell short of his family’s holiness, maintained in judgment the justice commended by divine law. Such was the power of reverence for unmistakable fairness! Consider, then, what evil your belief embraces: you attribute to God, whom we acknowledge as eternal, good, and just, an injustice that neither a king’s pride nor a bereaved son’s grief committed.

But let us press the point. It has been established that injustice cannot belong to God. It has also been established that he himself commanded that parents’ sins must not harm their children. The dignity of the one giving the command itself declared unjust what he forbids. Yet, to deal more generously with you, I give you the opportunity to answer. Of the two opinions I just placed face to face—parents’ sins should be charged to children, or should not be charged to them—which do you think should be regarded as just?

If you say your own, which you want applied even at the final judgment, I ask in turn whether you regard the remaining opinion, ours, as just or unjust. You will undoubtedly pronounce it unfair. But the law’s authority commands this very position to be maintained. You see, then, that one of three alternatives necessarily remains. Either you admit that God’s law is unjust—indeed, through the law, accuse God himself of injustice—or you resort to your teachers’ language and say that the law given through Moses was not commanded by your god. Or, if you dare say neither, you must admit that inherited sin is asserted against the law’s teaching and commands. Surely we cannot believe you capable of such madness as saying that God maintains justice in his commands but injustice in his judgments—or, according to your doctrine, justice in his judgments but teaches injustice in his commands. Although we dealt with this above, it was necessary to repeat it now.

added_allusions.reason: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

english: But if you say both are just, both what we say and what you say—that is, both what God’s law decreed and what Mani and the advocate of inherited sin invented—then, restraining the force of plain reason, we question you more gently and kindly. If you believe both what we say and what you say to be good, why have you stirred up all Italy with so much organized intrigue? Why have you hired crowds to raise riots in Rome? Why have you fed herds of horses throughout almost all Africa at the poor’s expense and sent them, with Alypius escorting them, to tribunes and centurions? Why have you corrupted worldly officials with the estates offered by wealthy women, so that the tinder of public fury would blaze against us? Why have you shattered the churches’ peace? Why have you stained a religious emperor’s reign with the wickedness of persecution, if we say nothing except what even you are forced to acknowledge as good?

Enough of gentler speech. The brightness of blazing reason now shows that evil and good, profane and sacred, godly and ungodly, just and unjust have no partnership. Therefore there is no conflict between God’s commands and judgments. Charging people with others’ sins is contrary to commanding that those same sins must not be charged to them. Of these two, accepting one necessarily excludes the other; showing one just shows the other unjust. Yet God’s law prescribes that parents’ sins must not be charged to their children (Deuteronomy 24:16). Consequently, by that same authority, its opposite—the theory of inherited sin—has collapsed completely, together with the Manichaeans.

added_allusions.reason: No partnership between justice and injustice.

english: I have certainly shown that what we defend is nothing other than what reason first identifies as entirely fair, what God then confirms in his law, and what, thirdly, was carried out with praise for the deed, precisely as we maintain the command should be understood. I have also repeatedly emphasized that this is true justice, which God showed to be pleasing to him by commanding it. Thus it has been established that the Manichaean transmission of sin finds no support either in reason or in the law’s testimonies.

added_allusions.reason: Recalls the command already quoted in section 12.
Recalls Amaziah carrying out the command, narrated in section 30.

english: But perhaps someone will be so obtuse as to demand explicit statements proving that God does not judge differently from the way he commanded judgment to be given. The demand itself is a wicked contention. Still, truth supplies weapons sufficient to satisfy every demand for proof, and I will gladly produce the strongest witnesses to this very point. Filled with the Holy Spirit, the prophet Ezekiel therefore says:

‘The Lord’s word came to me: Son of man, what do you mean by using this proverb in the land of Israel: The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel. All souls are mine: the father’s soul and the son’s soul alike—all souls are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.

‘But a man who is just, who practices judgment and justice, does not eat on the mountains or lift his eyes toward the objects of desire of the house of Israel; he does not defile his neighbor’s wife or approach a menstruating woman. He does not oppress anyone; he returns the debtor’s pledge and commits no robbery. He gives his bread to the hungry and clothes the naked. He does not lend his money at interest or take an excessive return. He keeps his hand from injustice and judges fairly between a man and his neighbor. He has walked in my commands and kept my ordinances by carrying them out. This man is just; he shall surely live, says the Lord God.

‘But suppose he fathers a corrupt son who sheds blood and commits sins. This son has not walked in the way of his just father; instead he has eaten on the mountains, defiled his neighbor’s wife, oppressed the needy and poor, committed robbery, and failed to return a pledge. He has fixed his eyes on idols and acted wickedly; he has lent at interest and taken an excessive return. This man shall not live. He has committed all these wicked deeds; he shall surely die. His blood shall be on himself.

‘But suppose this man fathers a son who sees all the sins his father has committed, is afraid, and does not act in the same way. He has not eaten on the mountains or lifted his eyes toward the objects of desire of the house of Israel. He has not defiled his neighbor’s wife or oppressed anyone. He has taken no pledge and committed no robbery. He has given his bread to the hungry and clothed the naked. He has kept his hand from wrongdoing, has taken neither interest nor an excessive return, has done justice, and has walked in my commands. This man shall not die for his father’s iniquities; he shall surely live. His father, however, because he inflicted suffering, committed robbery, and acted wrongly among my people, died in his own iniquity.

‘You have said: Why has the son not borne his father’s iniquity? Because the son has practiced justice, judgment, and mercy; he has kept all my statutes and carried them out. He shall surely live. But the soul that sins shall itself die. The son shall not bear his father’s injustice, nor shall the father bear his son’s injustice. The just person’s justice shall rest on himself, and the wicked person’s wickedness shall rest on himself.

‘If a wicked person turns away from all the iniquities he has committed, keeps all my commands, and practices judgment, justice, and mercy, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of the offenses he committed shall be remembered. Through the justice he has practiced he shall surely live. Do I really desire the wicked person’s death, says the Lord God, rather than that he turn from his evil way and live?

‘But if the just person turns away from his justice and commits iniquities, acting according to all the iniquities the wicked person has committed, he shall not live. None of the righteous deeds he has done shall be remembered. In the offense by which he fell, and in the sins he committed, he shall die.

‘You have said: The Lord’s way is not right. Listen now, house of Israel: Is my way not right? Rather, your way is not fair. When the just person turns away from his justice and commits an offense, he shall die in the offense he committed; in that very offense he shall die. And when the wicked person turns away from the iniquity he committed and practices judgment and justice, he has preserved his soul and lives. Because he turned from all the iniquities he committed, he shall surely live and shall not die.

‘The house of Israel says: The Lord’s way is not right. Is my way not right, house of Israel? Is it not rather your way that is not right? Therefore I will judge each of you according to your own ways, house of Israel, says the Lord God’ (Ezekiel 18:1–30).

Does God not appear a fully competent defender of his own judgments, when on this question he has not only passed judgment but also reasoned through so many points? Clearly, foreseeing the errors of our times, he justly and providently accomplished two things through the brightness and abundance of his words. First, no one should be unsettled by any ambiguity in the questions. Second, those who willingly plunged into shipwreck should have no plank of excuse remaining.

He speaks to the Jews, whose crimes had earned captivity. To divert the blame for their own disobedience, they claimed captivity was owed to their parents rather than to their own conduct. He confronts them with a father’s authority: ‘Why do you use this proverb: The parents ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel. All souls are mine: the father’s soul and the son’s soul alike—all souls are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:2–4).

To illustrate and confirm the fairness of his judgment, God uses an oath, adding a solemn pledge to the authority of his decree. The apostle understood this manner of speaking when he explained to the Hebrews: ‘God, wishing to show the heirs of the promise the unchangeable nature of his purpose, intervened with an oath, so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have the strongest encouragement’ (Hebrews 6:17–18).

He therefore says that these two things show God cannot lie: the fact that he promised, and the fact that he calls himself to witness that he will fulfill his promise. This does not mean that God’s word is normally weak or doubtful without such an attestation. Rather, to load his truth with weighty proofs, he adopted the kind of speech that makes even people accustomed to deceiving others believable. With this same weight God warns and commands in the present case: no one among his people should suspect what the advocates of inherited sin assert, and everyone should understand that God cannot judge in the way he condemns. ‘As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be spoken in Israel’ (Ezekiel 18:3).

What does ‘It shall no longer be spoken’ mean, when the Manichaeans still maintain it today with such effort? It means this: no one belonging to the people of Israel, or accepting this Scripture’s authority, will dare believe such a thing after my ruling. Anyone who persists in that opinion neither obeys these writings nor will be counted among the true Israel.

added_allusions.reason: Repeats the words that the proverb will no longer be spoken.
The distinction between Israel and true Israel may echo Paul’s distinction.

english: After exposing the emptiness of that proverb and ratifying his judgment by a divine declaration and oath, he also deigns to explain the reason for his justice: why relatives are not burdened with each other’s sins. ‘All souls are mine,’ he says; ‘the father’s soul and the son’s soul alike—all souls are mine. The soul that sins shall itself die’ (Ezekiel 18:4). Thus he also uses his ownership of souls to show why this measured judgment is perfectly fair.

He says: Since the father’s soul is mine and the son’s soul is mine, it is utterly unjust and foolish for my possession, my image, to be burdened with another’s deeds. This testimony, like many others, teaches that the soul owes nothing to reproductive seed, since God claims it for his own authority.

added_allusions.reason: God calls the soul his image.
Repeats God’s ownership of the father’s and son’s souls.

english: I gave it this condition: no outsider could harm it against its will; instead it would freely embrace either sin or justice, either reward or guilt.

So you are angry with me because I believe God under oath rather than Mani dreaming! Especially since Mani produces no testimonies of sound faith, or even arguments of an alert intelligence. Such arguments could never be found strong enough to overthrow truth’s foundations; still, if aptly expressed, they might at least offer some immediate relief from the shame of stupidity.

God persists in strengthening by an oath what he had made sacred by a command. He goes on to make his decree plain through examples. Suppose, he says, a man maintains every form of justice with unstained devotion and fathers a son who clings to corrupt behavior and turns away from his father’s paths. The noble standing acquired by his father’s great devotion to justice does that son no good. Conversely, he presents this sinner’s son avoiding his father’s ways by a better decision, and shows that his parent’s iniquity does him no harm. He places justice and sin on an equal footing, asserting that parents’ vices no more travel through reproductive seed than virtues can. All souls belong to his authority. This also exposes the irreverence of your claim that newborn children’s souls and bodies belong to the devil’s dominion.

added_allusions.reason: Just father, wicked son, and just grandson.

english: Having established the balanced scales of his judgment, he was already condemning your opinion in people who thought similarly. ‘You have said: Why has the son not borne his father’s iniquity? Because,’ he says, ‘the soul that sins shall itself die. The son does not bear his father’s injustice, nor does the father bear his son’s injustice. The just person’s justice shall rest on himself, and the wicked person’s wickedness shall rest on himself’ (Ezekiel 18:19–20). Which of us could ever have discussed this with as much care as God did through his prophet’s mouth, distinguishing, comparing, and repeating the points?

He declares that past errors do not harm even the very people who sinned voluntarily, if they turn to repentance and reform. ‘If the wicked person turns away from the iniquities he committed and keeps my commands, none of the offenses he committed shall be remembered. Through the justice he has practiced he shall surely live’ (Ezekiel 18:21–22). That is: Since my merciful purpose is to forgive even people’s own sins when they reform, how could I charge newborn children with someone else’s? Or could things be so arranged that innocence is guilty before me when it is created, although it has power with me when it is recovered after having been interrupted?

This displeased idol worshipers; and our faith, which you see shaped by this law, displeases you too. Those irreverent people therefore said: ‘The Lord’s way is not right.’ ‘Listen, then, house of Israel,’ he says. ‘Is my way not right? Is it not your way that is unfair? Therefore I will judge each of you according to your own way, says the Lord God’ (Ezekiel 18:29–30).

Do you see the testimonies defending us? Are we chasing ambiguities? Are we hunting for vague phrases? Are we defending faith with weak or tangled arguments? The just person’s justice shall rest on himself, and the wicked person’s wickedness shall rest on himself’ (Ezekiel 18:20). The way God promises to judge shines clearly: he charges neither children with their parents’ sins nor parents with their children’s. Thus Scripture’s testimony has also established what reason would not allow to be doubted: God maintains in his judgments the same justice he maintained in his commands.

Does it mean that parents’ offenses harm neither adult nor newborn children? Or that they are prevented from harming only those already older and practicing justice, while little children, before draining away the natural poison through their own justice, are burdened by their parents’ crime—so that the very thing God denied through the prophet actually happens?

Since you see that his denial opposes your reasoning and insist that it is false concerning infants, refute both its parts by the condition of newborn children. english: You do not think the reproductive seed of all people is polluted by the guilt of an act of will; yet you claim this justice has no force in the case of Adam’s crime alone, and his is the one sin charged to everyone. I do not know how to respond first. Should I laugh, as your extraordinary absurdities demand? But the destruction of the many people you deceive calls for pity and tears. Should I therefore be overcome by earnest grief? Yet your monstrous arguments provoke laughter even in a sorrowful mind.

If this age has any time left, who will be able to believe the written record that there existed a man who believed and swore that what was natural was not natural, that what belonged to generation did not belong to generation, and that what affected certain people solely because they were parents did not belong to the condition of parents? I think a future generation will consider these claims invented rather than defended by any mortal.

These are the lurchings, nausea, and vomitings your party and belief undergo. You say: Parents’ sins cannot flow to their children through nature, because an act of choice is not bound to reproductive seed; but Adam’s sin, conceived by his will, passes through nature to all people, because an act of choice is bound to reproductive seed. Again: God does not condemn children for their parents’ sins, because that is the height of injustice; but he condemns Adam’s descendants for their parents’ sin, which no justice can defend. Finally: What applied to Adam only because he fathered children under the law of marriage does not belong to the condition of generation by which spouses become parents.

Is this steering a course, or floundering? Is this digesting an argument, or feeling sick? Is this taking in anything solid, or constantly vomiting? In the same words you affirm what you denied; in the same lines you deny what you affirmed. And you are angry that we do not submit to a man so shattered by serious illness that he cannot retain what he takes in!

english: Even you see that this is not worth disputing. Still, we must help unwary minds that seize on the crudest opinions, flattering bad conduct, to comfort a wounded conscience. We therefore ask whether you discovered any occasion in Scripture for an invention of such stupidity. If you say, ‘Through one man sin entered the world’ (Romans 5:12), we remind you to reread the preceding book of this work. If you remember it, you will be unable to appropriate the apostle’s testimony.

If, however, you say that one form of baptism consecrates people of different ages, you will admit, even if I say nothing, that it contains no mention of infected generation, diabolical flesh, or Adam. Although this does not concern the transmission of sin, we shall nevertheless answer it fully in its own place.

Produce, then, at least one pronouncement of the law against the great authority of the witnesses we have brought forward, against manifest justice and clear reason—a pronouncement through which you can show you were deceived. I add that last phrase because even if some passage seemed, through ambiguous wording, to indicate such a thing, the brilliance and teaching of other pronouncements would compel it to be explained in a way consistent with justice.

But as it is, not even a slight occasion for this opinion can be found in the holy Scriptures. On the other side, the faith we defend is fortified by examples and testimonies no less than by its own reasons. You are therefore completely possessed by a deadly obstinacy, believing that Manichaean dreams must be accepted at the expense of law, reason, wisdom, and justice.

Still, attend to what we bring against this view. Even if you could prove that Adam’s sin is charged to his children, you would nonetheless agree that other parents’ crimes do not harm their offspring.

english: It would therefore be clear that it was not generation but some other cause that made children appear liable for the sin of this one parent—before an unjust judge, however.

Thus, just as the judge’s reputation would be stained by condemning the innocent, the condition of generation would be vindicated by the examples of other parents. For if the source of the transmission and the guilt lay in the work of reproduction, that condition would pollute all reproduction.

But if the outcomes differed although the mode of generation did not, it would become entirely clear that even in the marriage whose guilt its offspring had shared, generation itself had not been corrupted.

What, then, have we established? That the nonexistence of inherited sin is so certain that, even if you showed children punished for Adam’s sin, it would still be established that sins cannot be inborn and guilt cannot travel with reproductive seed, since you would admit that this does not happen in all reproduction. Consequently, even if vices were handed on to persons, they would not be mixed into conception.

But as it stands, you and I agree that a parent’s sin could not pass to children except through corruption and guilt in generation itself. Reason, examples, and the law agree that the condition of generation cannot possibly have been corrupted. Your own concession confirms this, for you say that no parents’ sins except those of two people pass to their children. It has therefore been established beyond defeat that the devil neither corrupted the first humans’ reproductive power nor made any sin capable of being born.

We are asked, then, why we do not agree that sin is natural. We answer: Because the idea has no appearance of plausibility, much less truth, no appearance of justice or piety; because it makes the devil appear to be humanity’s creator.
Because it fastens the charge of injustice upon God as judge.
Because it weakens and destroys free will, the chief defense protecting Christ’s Church against various errors.
By saying that all people are so incapable of any virtue that they are filled with ancient crimes inside their mothers’ wombs.
Yet you invent a power for these crimes that not only drives out natural innocence but also afterward compels people throughout their entire lives into every vice.

You swear that this law of sin remained and flourished even in the prophets and apostles, already illustrious through the great brilliance of their conduct and miracles, and even after the grace of Christ’s mysteries—which you suppose comes to the aid of all these outrages of your doctrine.

english: Because it extinguishes efforts toward every kind of honorable conduct; because it comforts and increases moral obscenity by defaming God’s works, that is, human nature; because it exposes all the law’s commands to the charge of demanding the impossible—that is, to the charge of injustice.
Because it contains no less indecency than irreverence, embracing shame concerning the genitals as its chief evidence.
And because, in place of sacred authorities, it swells with accusations against God.
It claims there is tyrannical excess in his commands.
Savage injustice in his judgments.
And Punic deceit in his oaths.

english: Because, in place of arguments and every kind of logical demonstration, it relies on Mani’s dreams and madness.
These, then, are the reasons that fire us to attack natural evil and make us disdain and despise association with the ruined.

They ensure that all the world’s uproar frightens us no more than the sight of a rustling stand of bitter lupines shaken by filthy pigs or gusts of wind. [Literary allusion: Virgil, Georgics 1.75–76.]

We therefore believe God to be just, good, and truthful. Consequently, we maintain that his law has commanded nothing impossible, his testimonies confirm nothing false, and his judgments pronounce nothing unjust. He himself is the creator of human beings, whom he creates liable to no crime, but full of natural innocence and capable of voluntary virtues.

Taken together, these points require one of two conclusions: either God must be believed to be what the Manichaean advocate of inherited sin invents, or you, together with everyone accepting the doctrine of inherited sin, must be recognized as the kind of person the God we honor opposes. But God cannot be what Mani dreams. He is the good, just, and true God whom all holy Scripture, the whole law, and our faith worship. Consequently, such is your doctrine that, just as it is accepted by dishonoring God, it is destroyed by honoring him.

It is time to move on to other matters. Yet the importance of the case requires us to supply even what we think we passed over in the preceding book. A sensible reader may judge this unnecessary. Still, experience shows that a case brought low by its dangers clings even to slight supports. It is worth taking away the consolations of those whose defenses you have removed.

When we came to the apostle Paul’s statement that the advocate of inherited sin used to peddle to people unfamiliar with Scripture—‘Through one man sin entered the world’ (Romans 5:12; see this work 2.56–57)—I first showed that the wording itself excluded the advocates of inherited sin from the inner meaning of that passage. When the Teacher of the Gentiles traced sin’s antiquity, he placed a definite number as a powerful guard protecting generation. By saying sin entered the world through one man, he expressly indicated that he meant nothing about generation, which cannot occur except through two. I showed that a distinction had been made between parents’ sexual union and their sin: sin was indeed said to have entered the world, but through a number that could not apply to offspring. Throughout the book we argued sufficiently that the passage identifies not sin’s nature but its pattern, adopted by later transgressors through imitation, not generation.

Yet in the Letter to the Hebrews we read concerning the Jews: ‘They sprang from one, and him as good as dead’ (Hebrews 11:12)—that is, from Abraham. Earlier in the same letter, too, we read of Christ: ‘The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one’ (Hebrews 2:11). The advocate of inherited sin might seize on one of these texts, or similar ones if any can be found, and argue that it weakens our answer. We said that ‘one’ was used for the person through whom sin passed so as to exclude generation from the meaning, yet in this letter generation is indicated by the mention of ‘one.’ For this reason, I thought the matter should be reconsidered. I urge the reader to pay attention: this objection will be destroyed in several ways.

Where Abraham is mentioned, his wife Sarah is included too. Here is the sequence of the words: ‘By faith the one called Abraham obeyed the call to go out to a place he was to receive as an inheritance, and he went out without knowing where he was going. By faith he lived in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. For he was waiting for the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God. By faith Sarah herself, though barren, received power to conceive seed even beyond the usual age, because she believed the one who promised was faithful. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, there sprang descendants as numerous as the stars of heaven and as countless as the sand along the seashore’ (Hebrews 11:8–12).

After mentioning both Abraham and Sarah, and saying that she was past childbearing through old age but received the power to conceive seed by faith, he could confidently add that from one arose so many people, comparable in number to the stars. Both praise of the faithful and the truth of the event required the parents’ union to be described. But the art of praise prompted him, in commending the multitude descended from those two, to name one rather than both. He wanted to show how much steadfast faith had gained. Saying that God’s power had produced a multitude beyond counting, he judged it more fitting to praise God’s work by calling them descendants of one rather than two. This was especially so because the added praise in the final expression caused no loss to historical accuracy: he had already supplied that accuracy by mentioning both persons.

In Hebrews, then, where generation is the subject, many are said to have arisen ‘from one.’ In Romans, however, where the apostle discusses sin, he says sin entered ‘through one man.’ By that number he taught with complete clarity that he meant nothing about generation.

english: Where it is said of Christ, ‘The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one’ (Hebrews 2:11), this can be understood as referring not to Adam but to God, by whose power Christ according to the flesh and the whole human race were made. Consequently, the similarity of other expressions has contributed nothing to undermine the apostle’s meaning when he said that sin entered the world through one man.

Yet what follows should stay firmly in the sensible reader’s mind: understand that so far I have argued far more leniently than the matter required. Let us allow that many testimonies show generation, which cannot happen except through two, is nevertheless commonly said to occur through one. The theory of inherited sin will still gain nothing. Why? Because some expressions are figurative or extended, and others are proper and exact. Things with proper names can lend their terms without suffering loss. But things spoken of in a borrowed sense are not allowed to impose the implications of their own definitions on the primary things to which the terms properly belong. All this happens without fault when we lend words to matters about which there is no doubt.

english: But let us return to the book he addressed to Valerius, in which he selected statements from just one of my books for discussion and refutation. In the first book of the present work I had reached those statements of Augustine where his shamelessness was uncovered. Trying to escape the odium of an opinion that would seem to make the devil humanity’s creator, he declared that God is the author of evils and himself creates a substance of such a character that it incurs guilt before it acquires the use of reason, and is placed in the devil’s kingdom by its Creator’s hands.
And that God is the potter fashioning vessels of wrath and destruction (Romans 9:22).

english: I filled the second book with an exposition of the apostle, setting Augustine’s arguments against it, to the extent truth supplied me the ability. So now let us return to the sequence of his book.

After putting forward one passage from the brief preface of my earlier work as though to attack it, and adding his claim about his god as the potter of sinners, he accuses me. Let his own words display how consistent and straightforward he is:

‘It is not, then, as you say while deceiving yourself and others, that anyone who says humans have free will or that God creates newborn children is called a Caelestian and Pelagian. The catholic faith says these things too. But anyone who says humans have free will to worship God rightly without God’s help, and anyone who calls God the creator of newborn children in such a way as to deny that he redeems infants from the devil’s power, is called a Caelestian and Pelagian. Both of us, therefore, say that humans have free will and God is the creator of newborn children. That is not why you are Caelestians and Pelagians. But that anyone is free to do good without God’s help, and that infants are not rescued from the power of darkness and thus transferred into God’s kingdom—these are your claims. That is why you are Caelestians and Pelagians’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.8; compare Colossians 1:13).
I have frequently shown you floundering in the swamp of your irreverence and fear; a sensible reader surely will not doubt it.

In the first book, therefore, I showed that I had not lied when I wrote that everyone who fled the stigma of association with us fell over the precipices of the Manichaeans, who deny free will and God as humanity’s creator. I also showed that you immediately embraced, in entirely explicit language, what you had attempted to repel, even quoting the writings you sent to Boniface (see this work 1.14). Yet this answer of yours, which I have just quoted, admits the same thing. You said the catholic faith believes both in free will and in God as the creator of newborn children. Among all heretics, the Manichaeans are certainly the ones who deny both, along with you.

But stripped of the substance of catholic faith, you put on its name alone like a thin cloak. You want us to believe that you too hold what catholics confess: that humans have free will and God creates newborn children. If you said this straightforwardly and faithfully, end the dispute by falling silent. Let the reputation of accusers return to us for having charged you with what your confident denial has erased. Add only this to your declaration: if any sect or argument is found trying by some reasoning to overthrow this twofold confession, which you have professed catholic, it is either not yours or no longer defended by you.
If you prefer to defend by substantial argument your denial of the positions in question, explain the definitions of free will and surround its boundaries, as with markers, by precise distinctions.
And also maintain that God creates the kind of human beings fitting for his hands and his justice.

You have certainly done neither. After replying that catholics acknowledge free will—and pretending to be one of them—you immediately added a definition taking away what you seemed to have granted. For you say: ‘But anyone who says humans have free will to worship God rightly without his help is called a Pelagian.’ And again: ‘We say that humans have free will; but you say that anyone is free to do good’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.8).

When you claim we say everyone’s freedom of choice is sufficient to worship God rightly without his help, you are lying outright. Worship of God is understood in many ways: keeping the commands, condemning vices, simplicity of life, the ordering of sacred mysteries, and the depth of doctrines Christian faith embraces about the Trinity, the resurrection, and many similar matters. How could we say without distinction that free will is sufficient to worship him without God’s help, when we read the Lord saying in the Gospel: ‘I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you hid these things from the wise and discerning and revealed them to little children. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing in your sight’ (Matthew 11:25–26)?

Freedom of choice could not discover on its own all these things, whether doctrines or mysteries. Natural reason, however, could teach people not to worship idols or despise God, who became known as the Creator of the world itself, as the Teacher of the Gentiles testifies (Romans 1:20). Neither we nor any sensible person, then, says what you invent. We maintain that God makes a human being with free will, helps that person through countless forms of divine grace, and leaves that person able either to keep God’s commands or to transgress them. This is where we defend free will: while God shows his kindness in so many ways—commanding, blessing, sanctifying, restraining, inviting, enlightening—each person already using reason is free either to keep or to despise God’s will.

We do not, then, believe that free will without God’s help is adequate for the worship offered by those initiated into the sacred mysteries. Rather, we acknowledge freedom of choice as a fully competent witness to divine fairness. When we must appear before Christ’s judgment seat and each receive what belongs to deeds done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Corinthians 5:10), God will be shown to judge nothing unjustly: he charges no one with a sin unless the person punished for it could also have avoided it.
