english: Your first statement, then, will gain nothing through its obscurity. Your second, in which you repeat that you acknowledge free will, yet do not believe any human being free to do good, has laid your whole inner self bare.

Look: just as we did in the first book, we now press you closely to show how you have not denied free will. Let our reader remember that you have admitted catholics proclaim free will and God as the creator of newborn children—two things no one but a Manichaean ever denied. Yet although we both granted these in common, neither you nor your doctrine leaves freedom of choice intact. It follows completely that you and your doctrine retain nothing of the catholic faith.

I ask, then: what is the power of free will, and what is its definition? Certainly it has no power to change natural conditions. No one ever changed the functions of the senses within himself—for example, receiving sounds through the nose or smells through the ears. No one changed the characteristic of his sex; no one could pass into the form of another animal or, through free will, replace his body hair with a naturally grown fleece. No one could claim a body of whatever quality or size he wished. We may extend these examples to everything falling under this condition.

Let us move, then, from natural things to external circumstances. Whose will controls fruitful fields, successful voyages, noble birth and riches, or the continued standing of that nobility, so that he could say God made him with free will to acquire these or similar things for himself? Natural conditions follow fixed orders; external circumstances are always carried along by uncertain chances.

Where, then, does free will reside—the thing by which humans surpass beasts, by which they were made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27), and on which alone the justice of divine judgment rests? Where, I ask, is this free will, which the Manichaeans certainly deny and which you yourself admit catholics affirm? Undoubtedly in a person’s ability, without any unavoidable compulsion from natural conditions, either to direct his will into wrongdoing or to hold it back from wrongdoing.

added_allusions.reason: Humanity made in God’s image.

english: To illuminate this clear matter with a few examples: a person is as free to choose sacrilege as to refuse it; as free to choose the murder of a parent as to refuse it; as free to choose adultery as to refuse it; as able to give truthful testimony as false; as free to obey God’s command as the devil’s persuasion.

In the preceding examples I emphasized a fully formed intention rather than the accomplishment of acts, because murder of a parent, sacrilege, adultery, and similar deeds are easier to avoid than to commit. An evil will does not always have the opportunity to carry out what it wants. Conversely, abstaining from these things involves complete quiet—unless you call the very unwillingness to toil a kind of toil. I pass over what holy Scripture, presented by prophets, evangelists, and apostles, and teachers shining with catholic soundness—John, Basil, Theodore, and others like them—have commended: committing crimes takes much greater effort than avoiding them.

For now I stress what concerns the present question: free will was given for no other purpose, and can be understood in no other way, than that no one is dragged with a captive will either toward justice or toward injustice.

Vices certainly have sweet enticements, and punishments inflicted by persecutors often bring bitter tortures. But the judgment of honor beats back the former, and the greatness of patience overcomes the latter.

Yet possessing virtues is not a wretched business. Besides a kind of kingdom in a good conscience, it enjoys the promised height of eternal blessedness. The aids of God’s grace are also present, never abandoning the will on virtue’s side. Although grace has countless forms, they are always applied with such restraint that they never displace free will. They offer support for as long as the will chooses to lean on them, without overpowering a resistant mind. That is why, just as some people rise from vices to virtues, others also fall back from virtues to vices.
How, then, do you acknowledge free will when you say it can do only one thing—evil—but cannot turn away from evil and do good (Psalm 34:14; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 33:15)?
For now I say nothing about the frenzy with which you rage against the whole law, believing that it commanded mortals things it saw they had no capacity to do.

Instead I ask: with which poets did you stumble upon a Hippocrene like this, to invent a two-part beast—not by composing poetry but by blaspheming—whose body you fashioned from an evil necessity while coating only its face with the name of freedom?
For in the work you sent to Rome you argue this way too: ‘The will, which is free in evil things, is not free in good things’ (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 1.7).

And here you call someone a Caelestian for believing that anyone is free to do good. You therefore call free what you insist can do nothing but evil. Find, if you can, another definition of something unfree, and claim this as free! Even if you had lost your senses so completely that you could not see freedom’s definition in the thing itself, ought you not to have understood freedom’s essence from its opposite?

Suppose you were similarly uncertain what eyesight meant and defined it as follows: Sight means having the eyes gouged out, or being unable to see anything through some obstruction when it is time to see. Suppose you thought this definition fitted sight, but then turned to explain its opposite, blindness. You could find no other explanation except that, in an animal whose nature includes eyesight, the eyes have been gouged out or blocked by thick fluid, taking away the ability to see. You would surely come to your senses and recognize that one definition cannot fit contrary things.

Then, if blindness could mean only the deprivation of sight in an animal’s eye when it should be able to see, the definition of sight would emerge by denying the conditions used to explain blindness. Sight would be the proper capacity to see at the appropriate time, with eyes neither gouged out nor blocked. If you stubbornly resisted after this was shown, you would achieve only this: listeners would either think you opposed your own conscience with shameful obstinacy, or, if you convinced them that you really thought this way, they would judge your mind’s eyes as thoroughly gouged out as those of the person you had defined as possessing sight.

To apply the example to our case, then: you could have understood what to call free from the definition of unfree. Even if your understanding grew dark when defining free will, so that you thought something could be called free while confined to one of two opposites, you should have noticed that captivity—that is, lack of freedom—can be explained only as being bound to one of two opposites. Freedom must therefore be named by denying captivity. Since what is unfree is forced to cling to one of the opposites, its contrary, what is free, cannot be bound to either.

Since this is so, and you resist this point so miserably, it is uncertain which judgment better fits you: that you defend falsehood against your conscience, or think what is false to be true. Thus whether you have lost the eyes of reason remains uncertain, while it is certain that you have lost the eyes of faith.

To repeat our conclusions briefly: free will is assisted on evil’s side by the pleasures of vice or the devil’s persuasions, and on good’s side by teachings of virtue and the various forms of divine grace. It cannot exist unless necessity is removed from it in respect of both justice and sin.
Catholics acknowledge its reality. The advocates of inherited sin deny it, together with their teachers, the Manichaeans.

We therefore spoke truly: those deceived by you become Manichaeans to avoid being called heretics. Fearing a false disgrace, they incur a real crime, like wild animals surrounded by a line of feathers to drive them into nets, forced into actual destruction by an empty fear.

We call God the creator of newborn children in this sense: since it is certain that the God of catholics, who is the true God, can do nothing evil, the dignity of the maker himself forbids belief that the human beings he makes come from his hands unjust and guilty before they use their will. By denying one of these points you undermine both. You say you believe God is the creator, but the creator of evil human beings. Consequently you contradict your own doctrine when you deny asserting that the devil creates humans.
For when you attribute to God’s work the kind of beings he cannot make, you show that what you said he makes has nothing to do with God.

Although we dealt with this more fully in the first book (see this work 1.52, 64), let us briefly state your meaning here too. You fear assigning any substance to the devil’s work, yet you do not fear fastening a great crime—not merely some small fault—on God. Human flesh’s nature commands more reverence from you than God’s justice. You feared attributing human substance to the devil as though that were an important matter, but attached the formation of wickedness to God’s justice and holiness as though they were unimportant. As if, between two opinions that are both false, attributing flesh to the devil’s works would not be more tolerable than attributing iniquity to God’s works!

Just as you said here that God forms infants guilty and under the devil’s power, so in later parts of your book you vomited out something more repulsive than the Manichaean mysteries, saying about God: ‘He creates evil people in the same way as he feeds and nourishes evil people.’ [The source compares Isaiah 45:7.]
God, then, creates evil.
And innocent people are punished for what God does.
And the devil possesses them because God does this.
And God charges people with the crime of his own hands.
And what the devil weakly persuaded someone to do, God skillfully and persistently fashions, protects, preserves, and forms.
And God demands the fruit of goodness from a person in whom he implanted evil at birth.

added_allusions.reason: Demanding good fruit from an evil origin may evoke the good-tree and bad-tree comparison.

english: And afterward he lies throughout the whole law by saying that the Lord is just.
And one capable of so many crimes is still called God?

The Manichaeans’ memory will perish with a crash, because ‘the Lord remains forever; he has prepared his throne for judgment, and he himself will judge the world with fairness’ (Psalm 9:6–8; LXX/Vulgate Psalm 9:7–9). There is no crime in God. He therefore does not create evil people: if they were evil by nature, God could not create them. Consequently, just as confessing God as creator of good beings belongs to catholics, believing God the creator of evil beings belongs specifically to Manichaeans.
But let us examine the rest as well.

[Augustine writes:] ‘Listen briefly, then, to what this question involves. Catholics say that the good Creator God made human nature good, but, corrupted by sin, it needs Christ the physician. Manichaeans say human nature was not made good by God and then corrupted by sin. Rather, the prince of eternal darkness created humanity by mixing two natures that always existed, one good and the other evil. Caelestians and Pelagians say the good God made human nature good, but it is so healthy in newborn infants that at that age they do not need Christ’s medicine. Recognize, then, your own name in your doctrine, and stop charging the catholics who refute you with someone else’s doctrine and name. Truth refutes both the Manichaeans and you.

‘For it says to the Manichaeans: “Have you not read that the one who made humankind from the beginning made them male and female? For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. So they are no longer two but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined, let no human separate” (Matthew 19:4–6). Thus it shows that God both creates human beings and joins spouses, against the Manichaeans who deny both.

‘To you, however, it says: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). But you, excellent Christians, answer Christ: If you came to seek and save what was lost, you did not come to infants; they were not lost and were born safe. Go to older people. We lay down the rule for you from your own words: “The healthy do not need a physician, but the sick do” (Matthew 9:12).

‘Thus the Manichaean, who says an evil nature is mixed into humanity, at least wants the good soul saved from it by Christ. You, however, maintain that in infants, when their bodies are sound, Christ has nothing to save. Accordingly the Manichaean blames human nature in a detestable way, but you praise it in a cruel way. Whoever believes your praise will not offer their infants to the Savior’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.9).
I pointed out even in my first work that your chief aim is to be poorly understood.
And I showed that most of your inventions require almost more effort to understand than to defeat.
But if I wanted to do that with every point, I would seem needless by repeating the same things and lengthy by pursuing them all.

Everything you have published against us rushes toward one goal: persuading us that natural things are evil and that either the devil creates humans or God creates crimes. Still, I think brevity will gain something if I gather from different places into one account the chief arguments with which, when you wrap yourself in obscurity, you think you defend your whole opinion. I will first help them by an explanation, making clear what they attempt; then I will overthrow them, gathered rather than scattered, unfolded rather than tangled.
In the later parts of your book, after saying, ‘God creates evil people in the same way as he feeds and nourishes evil people,’ you add:

‘For what he gives them by creating them belongs to the goodness of nature. When he gives them growth by feeding and nourishing them, he gives good assistance not to their wickedness but to that same good nature which he, being good, created. Insofar as they are human, there is the good of nature, whose author is God. But insofar as they are born with sin and will perish unless reborn, this belongs to the seed cursed from the beginning by the fault of that ancient disobedience (compare Wisdom 12:11). Yet the maker of even the vessels of wrath uses this well to make known the riches of his glory in vessels of mercy (Romans 9:22–23). Thus, if anyone belonging to the same mass is freed by grace, he should not credit his own merits, but “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

‘Departing from this faith, this man refuses to allow that newborns are under the devil, so that infants will not be brought to Christ to be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom (Colossians 1:13). In this way he accuses the Church spread throughout the world, in which everywhere all infants about to be baptized are breathed upon in exorcism for no other reason than to cast the ruler of this world out of them’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.32–33; compare John 12:31).

Again, further down, you discuss sexual desire, without which spouses cannot unite. We defend it as natural and belonging to God’s work, not as some great good, but as a sensation of bodies made by God. You maintain that the devil implanted it in human inward parts, and, founding your doctrine on the shame surrounding it, you try to establish this in so many writings. About this same desire, then, as often elsewhere, you say in a later part of your book:

‘Therefore we do not criticize the honorable union of spouses because of the body’s shameful desire. Such union could have existed without any preceding commission of sin, and spouses would not have blushed for it. But this desire arose after sin, and their confusion forced them to cover it (Genesis 3:7). Hence later spouses, although using this evil well and lawfully, still avoid human sight during such an act. They thus acknowledge something shameful, although no one ought to be ashamed of something good. Therefore anyone who has lawful intercourse through shameful desire uses an evil well, while anyone who has unlawful intercourse uses an evil badly’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36).

added_allusions.reason: Vessels of wrath and mercy reveal glory.
Ruler of this world cast out.

english: [Augustine continues:] ‘For what makes both evil and good people blush is more rightly called evil than good. We do better to believe the apostle, who says, “Good does not dwell in my flesh” (Romans 7:18), than this man who calls it good.’

A little later you add: ‘Human nature, whether born from marriage or adultery, is God’s work. If it were evil, it should not be generated; if it had no evil, it should not be regenerated. To sum up both points in one word: if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved. Whoever says it is not good denies a good Creator to the nature that was created. Whoever denies it contains evil begrudges a merciful Savior to the nature that was corrupted. Therefore, in the birth of human beings, adultery must not be excused because of the good created from it by the good Creator; nor must marriage be condemned because of the evil that the merciful Savior must heal there’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36).

I have quoted these many passages from your writings, in which you endured great labor of thought to seem to say something clever. In keeping with our practice of using no tricks, and in confidence in the truth, they ought to be distinguished through our restatement, because your words are scarcely intelligible. You said, then, that the Manichaeans condemn flesh’s nature and maintain that humanity was made by mixing two natures, one good and the other evil. You said that we, whom you call heretics, say human nature was made by the good God and is good on its maker’s testimony, but is so healthy in infants that they do not need Christ’s medicine. Your own claim is that Adam’s nature was once good, made by the good God, but was corrupted by sin and therefore needs Christ’s medicine.

In the first book of this work I set your opinions beside the Manichaeans’ and showed that your faith differed in no way from their irreverence, from which it clearly sprang. There it appeared that fear unites you with Jovinian, but love wholly unites you with Mani. We must discuss this in the present context too, but first I distinguish our views, then yours. You correctly said we maintain that the good God made human nature good. But only this much is ours. You either failed to notice or suppressed one part needed to complete our position and inserted another of your own that is not ours. For we do not merely say God made human nature good in Adam. We say that in all infants it is created good by the same God who made that first human being. That is why we affirm that he creates all people.

You not only removed this part from our definition; in its place you inserted your own, which could arouse hostility at first glance but would disappear under examination. You wrote that we say nature was made good by the good God, but is so healthy that it does not need Christ’s medicine. See how short of truth you are, when you do not shrink from such obvious theft even in terms called opposites! Having first put ‘good nature,’ you then added ‘so healthy.’ Is ‘healthy’ the opposite of ‘good’?

Surely when we say ‘good,’ its proper opposite is nothing but ‘evil.’ If the subject requires us to say ‘healthy,’ we put ‘weak’ or ‘sick’ opposite it: if it is healthy, it is not weak; if weak, it is not healthy. But when we say ‘This is good,’ we identify its contrary with the word ‘evil,’ not with ‘healthy.’ You should therefore have said that we define human nature as created good by God, and as so good in infants that it needs no one to correct the way it was made. Or, if you preferred to indicate goodness by the different term ‘health,’ you should have marked the entire statement with consistent language.

Instead you slip like a little eel between the rocks of definitions. Truth forced you to admit that we call human nature good and made by the good God. Seeing much reason but no grounds for hostility in that part of the statement, you immediately shifted to other words, adding that we defend it as so healthy that we do not believe Christ’s medicine necessary for it. If you stumble into all this through ignorance, you prove utterly dull; if you do it by cunning, utterly crafty.
translator_notes: The web Latin text replaces two Greek terms with “YYYY.” The printed Migne Latin edition, PL 45, column 1306, preserves antitheta (opposites) and antitheton (opposite); the translation is confirmed against those printed terms, not solely inferred from the parallel Italian text or the context.

english: Here is my brief answer: far from denying Christ’s medicine to infants, whom we know to be innocent, we acknowledge that they especially need it in greater abundance. They are born tiny and weak, unable not only to feed themselves through their own labor but even to ask their parents for help. They are exposed to so many accidents that even milk that is too thick, and often the sleep of those nursing them, can cause their death.

Because their bodies are mortal, they also encounter the hardships of illness, the suffering of pain, and the dangers of disease. We therefore acknowledge Christ’s medicine as necessary not only to infants, whom he also made, but to the nature of all mortals.
Just as its infirmities are eased in this present life by various remedies, so they will also be removed completely at the coming resurrection—in the bodies of the righteous, however.

See, then, in how many respects we acknowledge Christ’s medicine necessary to human nature. But I know you will cry out that I am quibbling with you: you did not mean medicine that helps bodies; by ‘medicine’ you meant Christ’s grace, which you claimed we deny. You could be answered that this is your fault, since you refused to identify with proper terms what you wanted understood. Yet now that we have understood, even belatedly, which medicine you meant—the medicine you falsely and vaguely alleged we deny—let us answer this second point too. As we declared in our first work, we acknowledge Christ’s grace, that is, baptism, from the time Christ established its rite, to be necessary for all ages alike. We pronounce an eternal anathema on anyone who denies that it benefits even infants.

Since we repeatedly stress this in a clear profession, you are convicted of a public falsehood when you write that we defend human nature as so good that, being healthy in infants, it does not need Christ’s medicine.

Yet this grace, because it is also called medicine, makes some people good from being evil, while preserving the law of justice. But infants, whom God makes good by creating them, it makes better by renewing and adopting them.

added_allusions.reason: Renewal by baptism recalls the washing of regeneration and renewal.
Adoption by grace recalls the Pauline adoption language.

english: It is therefore clear that we do not deny the benefit of Christ’s grace to infants. What controversy remains, then, for which the advocate of inherited sin accuses us of error? That we do not agree that Adam’s nature was made good but everyone else’s evil? I freely acknowledge that we not only refuse to agree but attack this with all our strength. Put aside, then, those childishly twisted nets of your inventions and the popular bogeys through which you whispered that we deny Christ’s grace to the cradle. Let us contend over the central issue of the dispute. Following the order I promised, now that I have defended our views, let us weigh yours and those of Mani, whom you pretended to oppose.

He says, then, that the prince of darkness, the author of evil, created humanity by mixing two natures, good and evil. What do you say? That the good God indeed creates human beings, but creates them all evil.

Thus between you and Mani there is no disagreement about nature’s character, only about its author. You charge to God, whom you acknowledge as infants’ creator, the same evil Mani charges to the prince of darkness, whom he considered human nature’s maker. Little obstacle remains to renewing your alliance. Soon, however, I shall show that although neither of you shows any trace of truth, his statements agree with one another better than yours do.

What do we say? Undoubtedly something opposed to both of you: neither did the good God make an evil nature, nor did the prince of darkness make or mix another nature. Rather, the one God, author of all things, not only made human nature good at first but also makes it good in every newborn child. Yet we profess the help of its Creator to be both useful in many ways and necessary to it. The making of creatures is one matter and gifts another; and the work is not valued more highly here than the craftsman.

Both you and Mani therefore equally establish natural evil: you both call human nature evil, but he does so more consistently, you more deceitfully. Both of you suppose this evil was breathed by the devil into human inward parts. He exempts no one’s birth from it. You, however, to seem different in some way—although there is no difference—try to exempt just two human beings. Yet you do not free even their persons from sin. With the advance of a more learned intelligence, you say that what you persuade us became natural through them was not natural in them. So, lest your fraud escape punishment even here, the added stupidity punished the theft you committed against your teacher. To believe natural what you admit was adopted by the will is an invention not merely of an uneducated mind but of a drunken one. More about this elsewhere; for now, let us press the matter.

Mani maintains that evil is natural; you agree. He says sins are born; you consent. He says human nature is evil; you confirm this too. He says the nature of absolutely everyone; here you resist, asking that the first pair be set aside. Yet you do not vindicate even them from guilt; rather, you affirm that they originated natural evil. Even if we could indulge you in this, your teacher will not. Perhaps he will even punish your slow intelligence with a schoolmaster’s rod, forcing you either to submit to his authority or to leave his school altogether. Finally he draws his conclusion: an evil nature cannot have a good author. Therefore humanity, which both of you acknowledge to be naturally evil, is the work of the prince of darkness, that is, the devil.

But you rise up completely against this last point. Although you boarded the same ship as Mani and the same wind directed your course, once across the strait you thought you should nevertheless disembark on a different shore. Perhaps, however, choosing an immediate advantage may make hesitation tolerable, even if late. Into what harbor, then, do you steer your vessel? ‘I say,’ you answer, ‘that God is good, yet he also creates evil beings.’ What an escape from danger—straight onto the rocks! You wanted to pour the whole of Mani’s bilge over the one you consider God.
It is therefore perfectly clear that his opinion has more consistency: if something evil were created as such by nature, it would indicate an author resembling itself.
Truth, however, first lays down that what is as its nature compelled it to be cannot be called evil—that is, sin—and that sin is nothing other than a free will straying from the path of justice.
These defenses protect the innocent nature of all things, which, remaining as it was created, is proved liable to no crime.

Evil, then, cannot be natural. Consequently, no creature is guilty by nature, nor is its author evil. For evil is found not to be a subsisting nature. Just as every creature is good insofar as it is created, so God, the author of good natures, is proved entirely good, stained by no crime in his work. Everything Mani brought forward is therefore overthrown by this single catholic argument.

added_allusions.reason: Every creature is good repeats the scriptural affirmation.

english: Yet the man slain by the thunderbolt of such clear truth seems still to breathe in some respect when compared with you. His whole doctrinal structure collapses when only its foundation gives way. But three things in your case totter as his one does. Consider, then, whether any part of your building can rise.

Mani thought sin natural, though it can only be voluntary, and so laid his foundations in empty space. The rest he placed consistently alongside: since sin is natural, nature is evil; an evil thing cannot have a good author; therefore the whole human race must be attributed to the prince of darkness. All this could have stood, had truth not undermined his first claim: sin, a work of free will, cannot be shown natural, and whatever is natural cannot be sin.

By overthrowing his first definition, the wedge of reason brought his rooftops crashing to the ground. What hope have you, then, whose three claims stand on ground as slippery as his one? First you say sin is natural. Second, that God is good although he creates, shapes, and extends evils—that is, sins. Third, that an act of will has been mixed into reproductive seed. Each of these three heads of your definitions totters in itself. Totters, I say? Rather, like ropes made of sand, they fall apart before coming together.

One claim—natural sin—already lies destroyed in the direct defeat of Mani. The other two, peculiar to your opinion, fell in the same familiar destruction that struck him. If he could not establish that humans are born guilty through either an evil nature or the prince of darkness, how much more foolish are you, who added an accusation against God to demonstrate newborn children’s crimes! Just as nature cannot be sin—the thunderbolt that shattered Mani’s doctrine—so, conversely, what is sin cannot be natural. An act of will does not pass into the condition of a substance, as you suppose happened. Much more certainly, the good God never creates evil beings. Thus it has become clear that sin cannot exist in a newborn whom God creates.

The matter is clear and was sufficiently established in my first work. Yet because you wanted to be so deceitful as to attempt a distinction between yourself and Mani, I must now press the case. It must be clear that we have answered not only your past statements but also anything you may try to introduce afterward. We say, therefore, that God’s work in a newborn is so good that the natural characteristics of its substance need no corrector. Anyone who judges that what he acknowledges God made ought to have been made differently undoubtedly criticizes the one he acknowledges as the maker of a creature supposedly needing correction into another form.

Thus, while maintaining in every newborn the approval and measured praise due to created natures, we say that increases of divine benefits are useful and necessary to all ages alike. Yet neither virtue nor sin is attributed to anyone without that person’s own will.

God’s mercy is nevertheless shown still richer in this: he sanctifies infants who do not know it. That belongs to the praise of mercy, whereas their ignorance leaves them unstained by guilt; that belongs to the laws of fairness.

But I am speaking of the virtues we acquire through the use of fully developed reason. Since it was necessary to stress this here, as often elsewhere, I now urge the reader to attend to what follows. The reader will see that advocates of inherited sin differ from Manichaeans in nothing, offering against us as arguments only what is contained in their books. I already demonstrated this in the fourth book of my first work.

But since, after those books were published, a letter of Mani was found in Constantinople at your request, most blessed father Florus, and sent to these regions, it is worth inserting some of it. Everyone can then understand where these arguments for inherited sin originate.

In that first work I had already argued about fleshly desire or pleasure, also called lust, implanted in the sexes for the reproductive activity of generation. I showed that it is nothing other than one of the body’s instruments, implanted alike in rational and irrational beings and belonging to God’s work, since he equipped our flesh with sensations. Yet Augustine attacks it fiercely, calling it evil—that is, natural sin and the parent of every sin. He tries to persuade us chiefly from its shame, and mocks me for being ashamed to name it directly.

So I too will now briefly vindicate the character of this thing, which in my earlier writings I defended by making distinctions against Mani’s attack, by exposing its accusers—who nevertheless profess that they serve it unwillingly.
What your books contain, then, old Augustine, is this: ‘Desire arose after sin, and their confusion forced them to cover it’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36; compare Genesis 3:7).

added_allusions.reason: Covering nakedness after sin.

english: And again: ‘Anyone who has lawful intercourse through shameful desire uses an evil well; anyone who has unlawful intercourse uses an evil badly. For what makes both evil and good people blush is more rightly called evil than good. We do better to believe the apostle, who says: “Good does not dwell in my flesh”’ (Romans 7:18; Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). Elsewhere: ‘Desire is not the good of marriage, but the obscenity of sinners, the necessity of those who generate offspring, the heat of wantonness, the shame of marriage’ (Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.13). And this: ‘What they afterward did in producing offspring is the good of marriage; what they first covered in confusion is the evil of desire, which everywhere avoids being seen and seeks privacy out of shame’ (Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.8).

These and the other things you regularly use for this argument come more from your memory than your intelligence. Mani, then, labored to compose what he thought clever; you were disappointed in thinking you could conceal what you had read and retained.
Listen now, then, and recognize what your father writes to a certain daughter of his, your sister.

‘Mani, apostle of Jesus Christ, to his daughter Menoch. May grace and salvation be given you from our God, who truly is the true God. May he enlighten your mind and reveal his justice to you, because you are a fruit of divine stock.’ A little later: ‘Through them you too have been made radiant by recognizing what you were before and from what kind of souls you flowed—a kind mixed with all bodies and attached to flavors and various forms. For just as souls are generated from souls, so the body’s formation is drawn from bodily nature. Therefore, “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). Understand spirit, however, to mean soul: soul from soul, flesh from flesh.’
translator_notes: The source’s note 210 reads “Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.8,” although this passage is introduced by Julian as Mani’s letter to Menoch. The attribution is preserved here as a source-note irregularity, not substituted for Julian’s stated attribution.

english: You surely recognize how explicitly Mani affirms the transmission of souls by descent, and which testimony he uses to condemn flesh: precisely the one constantly on your lips, ‘What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit’ (John 3:6).

He therefore stresses, not merely by saying it but by repeating it, that belief in souls’ transmission by descent is characteristic of his doctrine. He also tries to establish it through the analogy of bodies generating offspring: ‘Just as souls are generated from souls, so the body’s formation is drawn from bodily nature; and as flesh comes from flesh, so soul comes from soul.’ But let us proceed to the rest: ‘Just as God is the author of souls, so the devil, through desire, is the author of bodies. Thus, in the devil’s birdlime, through a woman’s desire, the devil snares not souls but bodies—’

added_allusions.reason: Continues Mani’s exposition of flesh from flesh and spirit from spirit, explicitly quoted in sections 172–173.

translator_notes: The final sentence is syntactically irregular in the transmitted web text. The translation preserves its stated links between the devil, desire, bodies, and the birdlime image; the quotation continues in the next section.

english: ‘Whether through sight, touch, hearing, smell, or taste. Remove, then, the root of this evil stock, and immediately you see yourself as spiritual. For Scripture says: “Desire is the root of all evils”’ (compare 1 Timothy 6:10).

You see in what spirit and for what doctrine Mani attacks fleshly desire, calling it the law of sin: if it were removed from bodies, his daughter, to whom he writes, would see that she had become spiritual. Let us hear which statements of the apostle he tries to use to establish this opinion: ‘“The flesh opposes the spirit,” because it is the daughter of desire; “and the spirit the flesh,” because it is the son of the soul’ (Galatians 5:17).

added_allusions.reason: The law of sin in bodily members.

translator_notes: The quotation attributed to Mani reads “desire,” not the usual “love of money” of 1 Timothy 6:10; its wording is deliberately preserved.

english: You understand that the innermost substance of Mani’s doctrine has been exposed—the substance from which your faith grows. Now he goes on to accuse us, that is, catholics: ‘See, then, how foolish they are who say this bodily formation was created by the good God, when they know it is generated by the spirit of desire.’

‘For they come together while the mind is unwilling, and act in secret shame. At that time they hate the light, so that their deeds will not be exposed (John 3:20). This is why the apostle says, “It is not of the one who wills” (Romans 9:16)—understand: this act. If we do good, it is not of the flesh, because “the works of the flesh are obvious: fornication,” and the rest (Galatians 5:19). If we do evil, it is not of the soul, because “the fruit of the spirit is peace and joy” (Galatians 5:22). Finally, the apostle also cries to the Romans: “I do not do the good I want, but I perform the evil I abhor” (Romans 7:19). You see the voice of the soul resisting desire and defending the soul’s freedom. It grieved because sin—that is, the devil—produced every desire within it (Romans 7:8). The law’s authority shows its evil by condemning all its uses, which the flesh admires and praises. Everything bitter to desire is sweet to the soul; through this the soul is nourished and summoned to strength. Indeed, the mind of someone restraining himself from every use of desire stays awake, grows rich, and increases; through the use of desire it usually diminishes.’

Do you now understand, even belatedly, that we have discovered the source not only of your thinking but of your language? You embrace your teacher with such love that you follow not merely his routes but even his footprints. All your writings assert this, as both the books you published under Marcellinus’s name and those you addressed to Valerius testify: this fleshly desire, which you also call shameful, was mixed into human bodies by the devil.

added_allusions.reason: Hating light lest deeds be exposed.
Sin produces every desire.

english: [You say] it is sin’s daughter and the mother of other sins, and that the apostle Paul complains about it when he says, ‘I know that good does not dwell in my flesh’ (Romans 7:18), and, ‘I do not do the good I want, but do what I hate’ (Romans 7:15). Catholics have always explained this as blaming habit, not defaming nature.
Yet by argument and by appropriating Scripture’s testimonies, you maintain that this desire, which you call the law of sin, both polluted him and all the saints and drew their complaints.

added_allusions.reason: Explicit law-of-sin terminology.

english: What does Mani say? ‘The devil creates bodies through desire. Through it he snares bodies, not souls. Remove the root of evil stock,’ he says, ‘and you will become spiritual. About this the apostle cries to the Romans: “I do not do the good I want, but I perform the evil I abhor”’ (Romans 7:19). He also calls us foolish for saying that this bodily formation belongs to God, although we acknowledge that it was generated through desire.

You see, then, how fully you and Mani agree in attacking us. You fight with his words, rely on his arguments, and call us liars for saying you not only were his disciple, as you yourself write, but still are. Yet even here he is more sensible. Believing this fleshly desire was introduced by the devil, he concluded that whatever appeared produced from diabolical desire must be acknowledged not to belong to God’s work.

You are duller: you call a human being the fruit of diabolical desire, yet assign him to God’s works. You do not say he was made good from evil, but that he is evil and produced from an evil root, yet has a good author—while the devil claims him as the fruit of his own root.

added_allusions.reason: An evil root and its evil fruit may echo the tree-and-fruit comparison.

english: For in your words, the devil rightly plucks all who are born from desire as fruit from his own tree (compare Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.26). You therefore revile us just as Mani does for maintaining that fleshly desire was created by God.

And that statement of yours, which I examined in my earlier work—‘Sometimes desire does not act when the mind is willing, although sometimes it acts when the mind is unwilling’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.7)—and your accusation of its arrogance because it stirs against the mind’s will: all this is expressed not merely in Mani’s ideas but in his words. Having criticized us for saying God makes human beings although we admit they are conceived through the pleasure of those coupling, he says: ‘Fools say what they know is generated by desire was created by God, although they couple while the mind is unwilling.’

As for your statement, ‘It is the evil of desire that everywhere avoids being seen and seeks privacy out of shame’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.8), Mani says the same: ‘They act in secret shame; at that time they hate the light, so that their deeds will not be exposed’ (John 3:20).

added_allusions.reason: Hating light lest deeds be exposed.

english: You say: ‘Anyone who has lawful intercourse through desire uses an evil well’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). You remind us to believe instead the apostle, who said good did not dwell in his flesh, and you want what is not good—that is, the evil dwelling in the apostle’s flesh—to be understood as fleshly desire (Romans 7:18). Mani put it no differently. After saying, ‘So that their deeds will not be exposed,’ he adds: ‘This is why the apostle cries to the Romans: “I do not do the good I want, but I perform the evil I abhor” (Romans 7:19). He grieved because sin—that is, the devil—produced every desire in him (Romans 7:8). The law’s authority shows desire’s evil by condemning every use of it, which the flesh admires and praises.’

added_allusions.reason: Sin produces every desire.
Repeats the clause that their deeds will not be exposed.

english: You thought it would be highly effective in maintaining a distinction between you and Mani to say that nature was indeed made good, but only in the first humans, while afterward it was entirely overthrown through desire. Mani argued this way too: ‘It is worth observing that the first soul, which flowed from the God of light, received this structure of the body to govern it with its bridle. The commandment came; sin, which had seemed captive, came to life again. The devil found his own limbs, brought the material of desire into the soul by deception, and through it killed the soul. The law is indeed holy—but holy for a holy soul; and the commandment is just and good—but for a just and good soul’ (compare Romans 7:9–12). Similarly in his letter to Patricius, he calls the first human ‘better than those who followed, as though made from the flower of the first substance.’

It is therefore no great thing, and contributes nothing to your defense, that you thought Adam should be excluded from the accusation against human nature. We shall soon discuss his condition more fully. Here it is enough to have shown that nothing in your ideas is so fresh that Mani has not already worn it out by rolling it over.

added_allusions.reason: Commandment arrives; sin revives, deceives, kills; law holy.

english: He persists in attacking us and adds: ‘As for those who have dared call this desire good against the evangelical and apostolic books, which they read to no purpose, you can see their saints sometimes sleeping with their daughters, sometimes carrying on with several concubines and wives. They do not see the apostle’s question: “What partnership is there between light and darkness, a believer and an unbeliever, Christ and Belial?” (2 Corinthians 6:14–15). They wander wrapped in desire’s cloud, enjoying its poison so much that, seized by madness, when they do this they think God has permitted it. As though they did not know the apostle said: “What they do in darkness is shameful even to mention”’ (Ephesians 5:12).

You surely see how he presses the matter of shame and thinks it tells powerfully against us, because we dare not call evil what we nevertheless acknowledge must be covered through modesty. Thus you have woven no garment to cover your doctrine’s deformity except the rags you accepted in your father and teacher’s inheritance.

He keeps rising up against us and turns directly to his opponent: ‘Come, defender of desire, describe its fruits and works in plain words. See, in opposing it I do not fear the light which it dreads and hates. “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his deeds will not be exposed” (John 3:20). Do you see that desire is the source of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust unwillingly, because this is the only thing we do while the mind is unwilling?’

This is the source of your own statement: ‘Why is it that moving the lips, tongue, hands, and the bending of the back, neck, and sides for their proper tasks lies in our power, but when it comes to sowing children, the organs created for this task do not obey? Instead we wait for desire, as though acting under its own authority, to stir them; sometimes it fails to act when the mind is willing, although sometimes it acts when the mind is unwilling’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 1.7). You listed the functions of all the bodily members, emphasized their obedience to the will’s command, and said desire’s activity is the only thing we do against the mind’s will. What does Mani say? ‘Do you see that desire is the source of evil, through which miserable souls serve lust unwillingly, because this is the only thing we do while the mind is unwilling?’

But let us see what else he adds: ‘Every sin is outside the body, because it consists in action; but the fornicator sins against his own body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Every sin does not exist before it is committed, and afterward only the memory of the act remains, not its actual form. But desire’s evil, because it is natural, exists before it is enacted, increases while it is enacted, and afterward both appears and remains.’ Why, then, quarrel with us for calling you a Manichaean, when his writings contain nothing but what you say, and yours nothing but what he wants to persuade us to believe?

And that saying circulating on ordinary people’s lips, though put there by you, is contained in this same letter of Mani: If sin is not natural, why are infants baptized, when they plainly have done no evil themselves? I said it flies over many people’s tongues because it is a more popular argument, understood even by the slowest. In your books, however, you place your entire hope on it. Your teacher develops this very point as follows: ‘I must ask them in these words: If every evil consists in action, why does anyone receive purification by water before doing evil, when he has done no evil personally? Or if he has not yet acted but needs purification, it is possible to show that they are by nature shoots of evil stock—those very people whose madness prevents them from understanding either what they say or what they confidently affirm’ (compare 1 Timothy 1:7).

Do you hear how he insults us? He calls us mad and unable to understand what we say or affirm, because we deny that people are shoots of evil stock, although we baptize in purifying water even those who have done no evil—that is, infants. Many passages from his statements have now been quoted. Yet if the heading did not name his daughter Menoch and Mani, who calls himself Christ’s apostle, they would altogether announce you as their author (see this work 3.172). Since you say nothing except what you learned from Mani’s teaching, do you think catholics should regard you differently from the man through whom you drank in the mysteries of these doctrines?

added_allusions.reason: Saints sleeping with daughters refers to Lot.
Not understanding what they say or affirm.
Patriarchs with concubines may refer, among other examples, to Abraham and Hagar.
Patriarchs with several wives may refer, among other examples, to Jacob’s marriages.

english: It remains to examine your statement which, promising to reduce it to one expression, you gathered up briefly—and, it must be admitted, rather cleverly: ‘If human nature were evil, it should not be generated; if it had no evil, it should not be regenerated. To sum up both in one word: if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36).

Here you must not be cheated of praise for your intelligence. From your standpoint it could not have been said better. Yet the nature of things prevents even precise cunning from accomplishing anything. It is altogether hard for you to kick against the goad (Acts 26:14). Whatever you put together melts like ice when the fire of truth is brought near. Now attend to our reply. You concluded: ‘Surely if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved.’ We agree; you spoke entirely truly. If it were evil, it ought not to be saved, because something evil by nature would neither deserve nor be capable of salvation. Why incapable? Because it could not become other than it had been made. Why undeserving? Because nothing in it would be worthy of deliverance by God’s mercy.

When we say ‘if it were’ about what certainly cannot exist, we are not giving hope that the denied possibility can occur. Rather, to destroy another opinion that arises, we commonly speak about impossible things. For example: If this or that existed, that consequence would undoubtedly follow. Since the first cannot exist, the conclusion introduced in order to remove it is denied all the more. We have already shown frequently that nothing can be evil by nature. Nevertheless, without prejudice to that settled point, we now approve the part of your statement saying, ‘If human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved.’

You located salvation in baptism and argued consistently that if the Manichaeans, who call nature evil, spoke truly, Christians would be foolish to believe baptism’s remedy should be applied to an evil nature. Thus anyone affirming that human nature is evil is forced to deny grace. This also works in reverse: anyone affirming grace praises human nature, understanding grace to have been provided for its salvation.

added_allusions.reason: Kicking against the goad.

english: Observe the conclusion: denying grace does not attach to praising human nature. Rather, these four positions are so connected that one cannot be maintained without the other: defaming nature produces denial of grace, and praising grace produces commendation of nature. These implications can run in either direction. You therefore spoke well: ‘If human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). The Manichaeans say both things: flesh’s nature is evil, and it neither can nor ought to be saved through grace.

But afterward you introduce the statement dear to you: ‘If no evil were within human nature, it would not need to be saved. Whoever says it is not good denies a good Creator to the nature created; whoever denies it contains evil begrudges a merciful Savior to the nature corrupted’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). Let the reader pay attention: you will see that he has said nothing other than what he had denied should be said. You have pronounced evil naturally present in the very thing you said was not naturally evil.
But an evil nature can mean nothing other than something having evil inborn within it.
To make the conclusion brief and plain: if evil exists in nature in such a way that evil is born from it with the reproductive seed itself, that nature is undoubtedly proved evil.

But if nature is vindicated from evils and defended as good, evil can neither be born from it nor naturally exist within it. Your conclusion has therefore vanished: the statement you introduced second did not distinguish itself from the first but duplicated it.

‘If human nature were evil,’ you say, ‘it ought not to be saved; if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). What have you shown except that one thing ought to be saved for the very reason you had denied that it ought to be saved?

Consequently you have come back to restoring by argument the Manichaean whom you despised in your profession. Saying, ‘If it were evil, it ought not to be saved,’ you assumed the appearance of fighting him. Adding, ‘But if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36), you showed that you serve him faithfully. It has therefore become clear that your pronouncement contains the same as Mani’s: human nature is evil, since both you and he say evil exists within it. And you have declared that an evil nature ought not to be saved. It has thus been established completely that your faith, with its forces wholly united to his, attacks both nature and grace.
It follows that no one can praise Christ’s grace without praising the Creator’s good work in nature.

Certainly the question here does not concern adults’ pursuits, but only the condition of newborns, in whom nature’s state is examined. Alongside Mani, you maintain that this nature, without any contribution from its own will, is guilty, condemned, and full of evils—that is, crimes. We defend it as guiltless, free from wickedness and the evil of sin, and capable of virtue.

Do you therefore charge this nature in infants with being criminal, corrupt, and condemned because of its own will or because of the condition of birth? If through its own will—so that those infants are said to have sinned by their own efforts—a monstrous opinion arises, but inherited sin is denied: someone did not receive from another what he could commit himself. But if it receives so many evils not by its own action but by its condition, it is proved naturally unjust.

Where, then, do you and Mani differ in your judgment of nature? ‘He admits it is evil,’ you say. If you deny that, then pronounce it good, and the dispute is over. Truth’s nets will immediately catch you for salvation. But you protest. Let us hear what you bring forth, Aristotle of the Carthaginians! ‘So much evil exists within it,’ you say, ‘that the devil possesses it and it deserves eternal fire.’
‘Yet it is so far from evil that no one but a Manichaean can accuse it.’
‘Nevertheless,’ he says, ‘I am no Manichaean, although I acquit it with words and condemn it with judgments.’

What should I accuse first here: the liar’s shamelessness, the debater’s appetite, or the irreverence of believing such perverse things? Yet I understand that we should use the prophet’s words: ‘We are blessed, Israel, because we know what pleases God’ (Baruch 4:4).
But the readers’ judgment will supply the task of denunciation; let us move on to the rest. Certainly among things there is no other evil that is truly evil except what we call sin.
From this sin, you say, natural evil is born in each person. Therefore nothing is truly evil except evil desert.

Mani calls nature evil for no other reason than that he considers it deserving of evil, and thinks punishments should be inflicted on it. You also affirm evil exists in human nature, and no different evil from Mani’s: fleshly desire, which you publicly proclaim was poured in by the devil. You say nature is so deserving of evil that you persist in sentencing it to eternal torments. Without doubt, then, you pronounce it utterly evil and condemned in exactly the same way as Mani.

Let us see, then, how the second part of your statement returns to this point too. You said: ‘Whoever says human nature is not good denies a good Creator to the nature created; whoever denies it contains evil begrudges a merciful Savior to the nature corrupted’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36). As you have been forced to profess, anyone denying that it is good also denies its good Creator, that is, God. And for nature to be evil means nothing other than to possess evil desert naturally. Thus even your confession supports our truth: you deny the good God as creator of humans, whose nature you swear is evil, appealing both to its vices and to its punishments.

We therefore do not begrudge a Savior to the nature we defend on the grounds of its Creator’s dignity. We deny that it is evil, so as not to become Manichaeans; we deny that evil is in it, so as not to be the very same Manichaeans under changed names.

We say that in each person already acting well or badly by personal choice, it is the person’s moral standing, not nature’s, that is corrupted. Accordingly we maintain that Christ’s grace heals what can be corrupted, since nothing is shown wounded except what is shown healed.
In those baptized, what is removed is not fleshly desire, which is natural, but the guilt of evil desire.
Consequently, the testimony of both the Creator and the Redeemer of the human race proves that no sin exists in nature.

english: To repeat our conclusions: by the testimony of both God’s commands and his judgments, I have shown that the theory of inherited sin is hostile to God’s justice.
By inserting Mani’s own writings, I have demonstrated that only a Manichaean accuses the fleshly desire God, the creator of bodies, implanted to bring the sexes together for reproduction.
I have shown that you have no arguments for inherited sin except those supplied by Mani.
Through examining your statement, I have exposed you as a denier of free will and of God as the creator of newborn children.
By explaining the statement you promised to compress into one word, I have proved that you pronounce nature evil.

I am therefore confident that even those slowest to understand, or deceived by favor toward you, can see clearly that you reject only Mani’s name. In everything you believe, along with all the followers of inherited sin, you cling to his doctrines, which are no less filthy than foolish.
